name.en: The Tel Dan Stele ('House of David')

modernLocation.en: Israel Museum, Jerusalem (found at Tel Dan, 1993-94)

corroborates.en: An Aramaic victory stele whose 'BYTDWD' is read by most scholars as 'House of David' — the earliest extra-biblical reference to the Davidic dynasty, c. 9th c. BC. A minority contest the reading.

King Mesha of Moab's inscription (c. 840 BC) recounting revolt against Israel; it names Omri king of Israel, YHWH, and the town of Nebo — paralleling 2 Kings 3. Some read a damaged line as 'House of David'.
Pharaoh Merneptah's victory stele (c. 1208 BC) carries the earliest known mention of 'Israel' as a people in Canaan — a fixed point for Israel's presence in the land by the late 13th c. BC.

modernLocation.en: Excavated near the Church of St Anne, Old City of Jerusalem

corroborates.en: A twin-pool complex with five porticoes matching John 5:2 — long doubted until excavation confirmed its form, a case where topographical detail in John was archaeologically vindicated.

name.en: The House of St Peter, Capernaum

modernLocation.en: Capernaum, on the Sea of Galilee (beneath the modern memorial church)

corroborates.en: A 1st-c. house singled out very early for veneration (graffiti, later octagonal church) and identified by tradition as Peter's house, where Jesus stayed and healed (Mark 1:29-31). The identification is traditional.

name.en: Hezekiah's Tunnel and the Siloam Inscription

modernLocation.en: Tunnel in the City of David; inscription in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums

corroborates.en: An 8th-c. BC water tunnel and its paleo-Hebrew inscription recording the diggers' meeting — matching Hezekiah's works before Sennacherib's siege (2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32:30).

modernLocation.en: Copies in the British Museum, Oriental Institute (Chicago), and Israel Museum

corroborates.en: Sennacherib's own account of his 701 BC campaign says he shut up Hezekiah 'like a bird in a cage' in Jerusalem — corroborating the siege of 2 Kings 18-19 while, tellingly, never claiming to take the city.

modernLocation.en: Found in the Ophel excavations, City of David, Jerusalem (2015)

corroborates.en: A clay seal impression reading 'Belonging to Hezekiah [son of] Ahaz, king of Judah' — a royal artifact naming a biblical king of Judah, from controlled excavation.

Cyrus the Great's proclamation (c. 539 BC) of restoring displaced peoples and their sanctuaries — the imperial policy behind the return from exile and the temple's rebuilding (Ezra 1; 6). Its direct bearing on Judah is inferred, not named.

modernLocation.en: Inscriptions from Cyprus, Pisidian Antioch, and Rome

corroborates.en: Several inscriptions attest the aristocratic Sergii Pauli family, consistent with the proconsul Sergius Paulus whom Paul met on Cyprus (Acts 13:7); which individual Luke names is debated.

disputes.en: Inscriptions confirm the family and its standing, but securely matching a specific attested Sergius Paulus to Luke's Cypriot proconsul is not possible; the identification is probable, not certain.
